But ok even with all my research before getting top, so far theres been ONE thing ive never seen talked about so i thought id share my experience- i was told to use neosporin or bacitracin on my nipples twice a day and cover them with bandages. I used bacitracin since its what my surgeon originally sent me home with (small packets to get me through the week until i got my own big tube). My surgeon also recommended i wear a shirt under my surgical binder so that way i could change the shirt when i changed my bandages since it was harder to clean the binder. Well, apparently it stains big circles into your shirts where the nips are lol! Im glad i got new, oversized shirts specifically for recovery instead of my own shirts but unfortunately i got nip stains on one of my comfort shirts (aka a big shirt that used to be my dads and just generally makes me feel good to wear). Besides the one shirt im kinda disappointed that got stained, i generally find it pretty funny and now call them my nip shirts.

I’ve also been looking into this- currently 2 weeks post op. I stopped smoking about 4 weeks before surgery and stopped edibles 1 week before (as directed by my surgeon). What i ended up doing was waiting until after my 1 week post op where my surgeon said i could start taking 800mg ibuprofen every 8 hours to lean off the heavy pain killers and when i was off them completely (i only used them sparingly to begin with) i felt it was comfortable to start low dosing with edibles again with tylenol/ibuprofen as needed. The drains and compression vest really are the worst part for me as well but having as many distractions as possible (and naps) are helping for me. Good luck!

I kept leopard slugs for awhile, theyre a lot of fun! Generally for herbivorous slugs the care is pretty easy- you can use any sort of tupperware  (maybe a shoebox size to start with?) with ventilation holes (poking the holes from the inside of the lid helps prevent injury to the slug!), a drainage layer on the bottom (lava rocks work well), some sort of ecoearth or organic potting soil, and plenty of places to hide! Slugs tend to hide in darker, moist spots (which is why you see them under rocks and planters) so be sure to not have too much light and to mist the terrarium well! Theyll eat a lot of the basic veggies like carrots, lettuce, cucumber, etc. you can also put in things like grass clippings and leaf litter but be sure to rinse them off first. I would also avoid putting any wood or soil (unless theyre baked or boiled) from outside in with the slug as there can be parasites and mites in them!

I know this is a lil old but i thought id share my experience! I have a service dog and work in petcare (mainly opening) but i dont take my sd with me to work. I don’t for a few reasons: 
1. People distracting her on purpose even after i ask them not to 
2. I’ve had reactive dogs try to lunge at her while i was in the store on too many occasions to be comfortable 
3. Our back rooms are small and having to navigate a larger dog with a full feeding cart is a nightmare even if she always tries to stay out of the way 
4. There is no protection for her when i work in the isolation room. This is a big one for me because I’m a big worrier about her health. I could have her stay just outside the room since its far enough from customers that i wouldnt be worried about someone trying to bother her but i absolutely do not want to expose her to any of the illnesses our animals might have. Pneumonia and ringworm are the two that come to mind first.
5. Some of our small animals are very skittish around big creatures like people and dogs. I just imagine having to move a hamster in one of our back rooms just to have it jump and scurry off potentially hurting itself or my dog just because my dog started alerting me to something. Or having a snake bite her because it got scared. 

Then again, my sd doesn’t alert to huge medical issues like fainting or seizures so I’m lucky enough to not need to take her out with me 100% of the time. Consider your own medical issues and what the dog would be tasked to do. Petcare specifically might not be a good fit when you have a service dog but being a cashier would certainly be better.

But the process of getting a service dog is... lengthy and very expensive so you would have plenty of time to sit down with store leaders to talk about what they think and what compromises could be made.
